title: HR Operations Excellence
tagline: Run the engine room of HR: clean records, accurate payroll, lawful policies, fair discipline and service people can trust.
description:
Every promise an organisation makes to its people is kept, or broken, by HR operations. The appointment letter, the payslip, the leave balance, the fair hearing and the reply to a simple request all come from the engine room. This certification teaches that work at professional level, using Pakistani workplaces, rupees and laws.

- **Lifecycle and records:** onboarding from offer to probation, personnel files, HRIS data, data protection and the monthly headcount reconciliation.
- **Payroll:** gross-to-net calculation, allowances, deductions, provident fund, gratuity, EOBI, provincial social security, overtime and income-tax withholding on salaries.
- **Law and policy:** the provincial labour-law landscape, Standing Orders, minimum wage, leave and working hours, handbooks and attendance management.
- **Employee relations:** grievances, show-cause notices, fair inquiries, proportionate penalties and the workplace-harassment law.
- **Service and control:** HR metrics with calculations, shared services and SLAs, compliance calendars and HR audits.

Each stage ends with a scored test and the final exam is tough, with calculations and realistic cases. Labour law and tax rules change often, so the course teaches you how they work and reminds you to check the current provincial law and Finance Act before you apply a figure.
audience: HR officers and executives who run onboarding, records, leave, attendance and payroll inputs
Payroll and HRIS specialists who want a firmer grip on the law and controls behind the numbers
HR managers and business partners responsible for policies, employee relations and compliance
Plant, branch and line managers who handle attendance, grievances and discipline in their teams
Professionals moving into HR from finance, administration or operations
outcomes: Run a compliant onboarding and keep personnel files and HRIS data complete, accurate and protected
Calculate gross-to-net pay, overtime, unpaid-leave deductions, gratuity and mid-year tax withholding correctly
Explain how provident fund, gratuity, EOBI and provincial social security work and who pays for what
Map the Pakistani labour-law landscape and write policies and leave rules that meet or beat the law
Handle grievances and disciplinary cases with a fair show-cause and inquiry process that stands up to challenge
Calculate and interpret turnover, absenteeism, time-to-fill, cost-per-hire and SLA compliance
Design tiered HR service delivery and run audits with root-cause analysis and corrective action plans

quest.name: The Ninety-Day Audit at Noorpur Foods
quest.premise: Noorpur Foods, a fast-growing snacks and dairy company with a head office in Lahore and a 1,200-person plant on Sheikhupura Road, has just been told that its biggest overseas buyer will run a social compliance audit in ninety days. Fail it, and the export contract that feeds half the plant goes. You have joined as HR Operations Manager. Behind the shiny brand you find missing files, a payroll nobody fully trusts, an outdated handbook and a shop floor close to boiling. Five stages, ninety days: put the engine room in order before the auditors walk through the gate.

badge.name: Noorpur Engine Room Marshal
badge.description: Awarded to professionals who proved they can run HR records, payroll, policy, employee relations and compliance to a demanding standard.

sessions.title: Onboarding, the Employee Lifecycle and HR Records
sessions.summary: See the whole employee lifecycle through HR operations eyes, run onboarding from offer to the end of probation, build complete personnel files, keep HRIS data clean and protected, and reconcile HR records with payroll every month.
objectives: Map the employee lifecycle and the HR operations work at each stage
Run a compliant onboarding from offer acceptance to the probation decision
Build complete personnel files and classify workers correctly
Keep HRIS data accurate, controlled and protected, and reconcile it with payroll

cards.title: Day one at the gate
cards.setting: Noorpur Foods plant, Sheikhupura Road. 8:10 am. Delivery trucks queue at the gate while the morning shift clocks in.

lines.text: Stage one of your quest begins at the front gate. Ninety days from today, auditors from Noorpur's biggest overseas buyer will walk through it.
Welcome aboard. I won't sugar-coat it: the buyer's audit decides the export contract, and our HR engine room has been running on WhatsApp and memory.
Example from this morning. Asif, a packing operator, has worked here three weeks. No appointment letter, no EOBI registration, and his CNIC copy is a blurry photo on my phone.
He works well. Paperwork can wait. I need hands on the line, not files in a cupboard.
There's a bigger problem. The HRIS says 1,240 active employees. Last month payroll paid 1,262 people. I can't explain the 22.
Twenty-two people we pay but cannot see. Your first mission: rebuild the front gate so nobody walks in, or out, without HR knowing. Where do you start?

cards.title: One person, one journey, one record

scenes.heading: The employee lifecycle
scenes.narration: Every employee travels the same road: attracted, hired, onboarded, managed and developed, rewarded, and finally exited. HR operations is the machinery that keeps that road paved.

scenes.heading: Data follows the person
scenes.narration: At each stage something is recorded: an offer, a joining date, a promotion, a transfer, a leave balance, a last working day. If the record is wrong, everything built on it goes wrong too.

scenes.heading: Joiners, movers, leavers
scenes.narration: Operations teams often call this the joiner, mover, leaver process. A joiner needs a record, pay and access. A mover needs changes with the right effective date. A leaver needs pay stopped, access removed and a final settlement.

scenes.heading: Where ghosts are born
scenes.narration: When a leaver is not recorded before payroll cut-off, salary keeps flowing. When a joiner is paid outside the system, nobody can verify them. Both create the gap Bilal found.

scenes.heading: The front gate
scenes.narration: So the front gate is not a guard post. It is a rule: nobody is paid, given access or put on a shift until their record is complete and approved.

cards.question: A candidate accepts an offer on the 3rd and joins on the 20th. Collecting her documents, verifying her CNIC and creating her HRIS record during that gap is called what?
options: Induction
Probation review
Pre-boarding
Requisition approval
cards.explanation: Pre-boarding is the work between offer acceptance and day one, so the person arrives to a ready record, a letter and access. Induction is the welcome and orientation that starts on or after the first day.

cards.title: Onboarding: from offer to probation decision
cards.body:
Treat onboarding as three phases, each with a checklist and an owner.

- **Pre-boarding (offer to day one):** signed offer, document collection, CNIC verification through an authorised service, education and reference checks with the candidate's consent, medical fitness where the job needs it, HRIS record created and approved, payroll and bank details set up, statutory registrations started.
- **Day one and induction:** written appointment letter signed, policies and handbook acknowledged, safety briefing, workstation and access, buddy assigned.
- **First 90 days:** objectives agreed in week one, documented check-ins, and a probation decision made **before** probation ends.

For workers covered by the Standing Orders law, terms must be given **in writing at appointment**, stating at least the classification, pay and key conditions. A letter promised "after probation" is a compliance gap, not a courtesy.

cards.caption: The HRIS is the single source of truth. Payroll and finance read from it; they never keep a separate employee list.

cards.title: HRIS essentials that prevent expensive mistakes
cards.body:
- **Unique employee ID** linked to the CNIC number, so one person can never exist twice.
- **Master data:** the core facts (name, CNIC, joining date, position, grade, pay, bank account) that other processes reuse.
- **Effective dating:** every change carries the date it takes effect, not the date it was typed. A raise approved in April but effective 1 March lets payroll calculate arrears.
- **Maker-checker:** one person enters, another approves. Nobody should both create an employee and approve their bank details.
- **Audit trail:** a log of who changed which field, when, from what to what.
- **Role-based access:** people see only what their job needs. A line manager sees team attendance, not colleagues' salaries or medical notes.
- **Monthly reconciliation:** active HRIS headcount must match the payroll register, and every difference is explained before payroll is approved.

cards.title: HRIS words in action
cards.prompt: Match each HRIS control to the problem it solves.

pairs.right: A promotion entered late still pays the correct arrears from the right month
One officer cannot add a fake employee and approve the bank account alone
An auditor can see who changed a basic salary in June and from what amount
A typing error cannot create the same person twice on payroll
A supervisor can approve team leave without seeing anyone's medical file
A gap between HRIS headcount and payroll is caught before salaries go out

cards.title: Hunting the twenty-two
cards.setting: Head office, Gulberg, Lahore. Bilal's two screens show the HRIS active list beside last month's payroll register.

lines.text: Matched by CNIC, not by name. Fifteen people left the plant in the last four months, but nobody sent their exit forms to HR before cut-off. They were still paid.
Four are new joiners Tariq sahib's supervisors added straight to payroll on a WhatsApp list. They work here, but they have no HRIS record.
And three are duplicates. Same person, CNIC typed with one digit wrong, so the system created a second employee.
Fine, problem solved. Delete the twenty-two from payroll and move on. The auditors will never know.
Delete four real workers' pay? And never ask where fifteen salaries went? Think carefully. What do we actually do next?

cards.title: Closing the gap the right way
cards.situation: Your reconciliation explains all 22 differences: 15 leavers still paid for up to four months, 4 genuine joiners paid without HRIS records, and 3 duplicate records. Payroll for this month runs in six days. Tariq wants all 22 simply deleted.

choices.text: Delete all 22 from payroll today so the numbers match before anyone asks
choices.outcome: The numbers match, but four real workers miss their pay and complain to Ghulam, and nobody learns where fifteen leavers' salaries went. You fixed the report, not the problem.

choices.text: Stop the 15 leavers and 3 duplicates, onboard the 4 joiners properly, trace where the overpaid salaries went, start recovery, and fix the exit trigger so it cannot recur
choices.outcome: Rukhsana nods. Each group gets the right treatment: real workers are protected, overpayments are traced (to the leavers' accounts or elsewhere) and recovered where possible, and the leaver process now starts in HRIS before cut-off.

choices.text: Stop the 15 leavers and 3 duplicates, and onboard the 4 joiners, but leave the past overpayments alone
choices.outcome: This month will be right, but four months of payments to leavers are unexplained. If any landed in someone else's account, that is possible fraud, and an auditor will ask what you did about it.

choices.text: Freeze the whole plant payroll until every file is perfect
choices.outcome: 1,200 people go unpaid over a records problem that affects 22. Wage-payment law and basic trust both suffer, and the shop floor erupts.

cards.title: The reconciliation, in numbers
cards.caption: Every difference is explained before payroll is approved. An unexplained difference is a stop sign, not a rounding error.

items.detail: People in last month's payroll register

items.label: Active in HRIS
items.detail: Approved active records at month-end

items.label: Leavers still paid

cards.front: Any manager can see any employee file. It's company property.
cards.back: Myth. Access should follow need-to-know. Managers see what their role requires; medical, harassment and salary details are restricted.

cards.front: Collect everything at joining, just in case.
cards.back: Myth. Collect only what you need for employment, pay, law and safety. Extra data is extra risk.

cards.front: Ex-employees can demand that every record is deleted immediately.
cards.back: Not quite. Keep what law, tax, pension and possible claims require for their retention periods; delete the rest on schedule and record why.

cards.front: Check references with the current employer without telling the candidate.
cards.back: Avoid it. Get the candidate's consent first; contacting a current employer unannounced can cost them their job.

cards.front: Does Pakistan have a dedicated personal data protection law?
cards.back: A dedicated law has been in draft for years. Check its current status, and meanwhile apply good practice: consent, minimum data, restricted access and secure storage.

cards.front: A WhatsApp photo of a CNIC is a fine record.
cards.back: No. Keep a clear, verified copy in the secure file system, not on personal phones, and verify the CNIC through an authorised service.

cards.question: In the HRIS, Bilal finds that the same payroll officer created a new employee and also approved that employee's bank account number. Which control has failed?
options: Effective dating
Maker-checker (segregation of duties)
Role-based access for line managers
Records retention schedule
cards.explanation: Maker-checker means one person enters a change and a different person approves it. When one person does both, a fictitious employee with a controlled bank account can be created without anyone noticing.

cards.title: Asif's file, fixed in a day
cards.body:
Saima uses Asif's case to pilot the new front gate.

- **Classification:** Asif fills a permanent packing post and has worked three weeks, so he is a **probationer**, provisionally employed in a permanent vacancy. Other classes used in the Standing Orders framework are permanent, badli (covering a permanent worker who is temporarily away), temporary (for work that will end), apprentice and contract.
- **Appointment letter:** issued that day, stating classification, pay, hours, probation period and notice. Asif signs, keeps a copy, and Saima files the original.
- **Records:** CNIC verified, clear copy filed; nomination forms signed; EOBI and social security registration submitted.
- **HRIS:** record created by Saima, approved by Bilal, joining date set to Asif's real first day, so his first three weeks are counted for leave and service.
- **Probation:** objectives agreed and a review date booked before probation ends.

Tariq loses Asif from the line for twenty minutes. Noorpur loses one audit finding.

cards.title: Five habits of a clean front gate
cards.body:
- **No record, no pay, no shift.** Payroll only pays approved HRIS records.
- **Exit before cut-off.** The leaver's last working day goes into HRIS the moment a resignation is accepted, not when clearance ends.
- **Match on CNIC, not names.** There are many Muhammad Aslams on a plant floor.
- **Real dates.** Backdating or forward-dating hides service and breaks leave and gratuity later.
- **Know the ghost signs:** several employees paid into one bank account, no attendance records, no verified CNIC.
- **Audit files monthly.** Sample ten and tick off each required document.

cards.question: Noorpur hires extra packers for three months to handle the Ramadan rush, with no permanent vacancy behind the posts. Under the Standing Orders classification, which class fits best?
options: Badli
Probationer
Temporary
Apprentice
cards.explanation: A temporary worker is engaged for work that is itself temporary and will end, like a seasonal rush. A badli covers a permanent worker who is away, and a probationer fills a permanent vacancy; neither applies here.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Front Gate
items: HR operations runs the whole lifecycle: hire, onboard, manage, reward, relate and exit. Each stage creates data that others depend on.
Onboarding has three phases: pre-boarding, day one and induction, and the first 90 days ending in a timely probation decision.
Give workers written terms at appointment, classify them correctly, and keep a complete personnel file with restricted items stored separately.
The HRIS is the single source of truth: unique ID on CNIC, effective dating, maker-checker, audit trail and role-based access.
Reconcile HRIS headcount with payroll every month, explain every difference, and fix the process that created it.

cards.prompt: Think about your own organisation. If you compared last month's payroll register with your active headcount today, matched by CNIC, would the numbers agree? Which part of your joiner or leaver process is most likely to create a gap?

quiz.question: Which phase of onboarding covers the period between a candidate accepting the offer and their first day at work?
options: Induction
Probation review
Pre-boarding
Workforce planning
quiz.explanation: Pre-boarding runs from offer acceptance to day one: documents, checks, HRIS record and registrations. Induction starts on or after the first day, and the probation review comes at the end of the first months.

quiz.question: A plant supervisor says new operators will receive appointment letters only after they pass probation, "to save paperwork on people who may leave." What should HR do?
options: Agree, but make sure the offer letter mentions the probation period
Issue written appointment letters with their terms at joining
Agree, provided the operators are registered in the HRIS on their first day
Issue letters after probation but backdate them to the joining date
quiz.explanation: Workers covered by the Standing Orders framework must receive written terms at appointment. An offer letter or an HRIS record does not replace them, and backdating a letter creates a false record.

quiz.question: Which of these belongs in a restricted confidential file rather than the core personnel file?
options: A medical fitness report from the panel doctor
The signed appointment letter stating pay and classification
Provident fund nomination forms
A verified copy of the CNIC
quiz.explanation: Medical information is sensitive and should be accessible only to those who need it, so it is stored separately. The appointment letter, nominations and CNIC copy are core employment records.

quiz.question: An increment approved in May is effective from 1 April. Which HRIS feature allows payroll to pay the April arrears automatically?
options: Maker-checker approval of the increment entry
Role-based access
Effective dating of the pay change
The audit trail
quiz.explanation: Effective dating records when a change takes effect, separately from when it was entered, so payroll can calculate the arrears for April. Maker-checker and the audit trail control and log the change but do not set its timing.

quiz.question: During a review you find that one HR officer can create a new employee record and also approve that employee's bank account details. What is the main risk?
options: Salary increments could be calculated from the wrong effective date each month
A fictitious employee could be paid into an account the officer controls
Line managers could see salary information they do not need
Personnel files could be kept longer than the retention schedule allows
quiz.explanation: Without maker-checker, one person can create a ghost employee and route pay to their own account. The other risks are real but are addressed by different controls.

quiz.question: The monthly reconciliation shows payroll paid 18 more people than the HRIS active list. Which explanation should be investigated first because it can mean money is leaving the company improperly?
options: Leavers who were still paid after their last working day
Employees whose job titles differ between the two systems
Employees whose leave balances were not yet updated
Joiners whose induction training is still pending
quiz.explanation: Leavers still on payroll mean salaries are being paid to people who no longer work there, which may also hide diversion of funds. Title mismatches, leave balances and training do not change who is paid.

quiz.question: A line manager asks HR for copies of all his team members' CNICs and home addresses "to send Eid greetings." What is the best response?
options: Share the CNIC copies but remove the home addresses
Share everything, since he manages these employees
Ask each employee to send the manager their CNIC copy directly
Decline, and offer to send the greetings through HR instead
quiz.explanation: Access follows need-to-know. Sending greetings does not require CNIC copies or addresses, and HR can achieve the purpose without disclosing personal data. Pushing employees to share it directly sidesteps the same principle.

quiz.question: In the classification used in the Standing Orders framework, what is a probationer?
options: A worker provisionally employed to fill a permanent vacancy
A worker covering a permanent worker who is temporarily absent
A worker engaged for work that will finish within a limited time
A learner paid an allowance while being trained
quiz.explanation: A probationer fills a permanent vacancy on a provisional basis. Covering an absent permanent worker describes a badli, short-term work describes a temporary worker, and a paid learner is an apprentice.

quiz.question: Which change to the leaver process best prevents salaries being paid after people leave?
options: Remove the leaver from payroll once the final settlement has been calculated and paid
Ask supervisors to send HR a WhatsApp list of leavers at month-end
Record the last working day in HRIS as soon as the exit is confirmed, before payroll cut-off
Check the payroll register against the HRIS once a year at audit time
quiz.explanation: Pay stops reliably only when the exit date is in the master record before cut-off. Waiting for final settlement or a month-end list leaves gaps, and an annual check finds problems months too late.

quiz.question: A shortlisted candidate for a finance manager role asks you not to contact her current employer yet. What should you do?
options: Contact her current employer anyway, because references must come from the latest job
Drop her from the shortlist, since refusing a reference is a red flag
Skip all reference checks because she has refused one
Respect it: use other referees, verify documents and make any offer conditional
quiz.explanation: Reference checks need the candidate's consent, and an unannounced call can cost her the current job. Other referees, document verification and a conditional offer protect the company without that harm.

sessions.title: Payroll from Gross to Net: Allowances, Deductions, Funds and Tax
sessions.summary: Open the payroll vault: build gross pay from basic and allowances, take it to net through lawful deductions, calculate overtime and unpaid leave, understand provident fund, gratuity, EOBI and social security, withhold income tax on salaries correctly and run the controls that keep payroll trusted.
objectives: Calculate gross pay, employee deductions, net pay and the employer's cost of an employee
Calculate overtime, unpaid-leave deductions and gratuity from stated rules
Explain how provident fund, gratuity, EOBI and provincial social security work and who pays
Apply the annual-projection method for income-tax withholding on salaries, including mid-year changes
Run payroll controls: cut-off, variance review, maker-checker and segregation of duties

cards.title: The WhatsApp storm
cards.setting: Payroll room, head office, Lahore. Bilal's phone buzzes non-stop. The plant workers' WhatsApp group has 340 unread messages.

lines.text: Stage two. The twenty-two are fixed, but closing them opened the payroll vault, and not everything inside is pretty.
Six months of night overtime, and the rate on the payslip is the same as a normal hour. Is that the law now? The boys are talking about a go-slow.
He's right, I checked. Someone set the plant overtime factor to 1 instead of 2 when we changed systems. And forty staff have provident fund taken on gross instead of basic.
And my own tax jumped in January after my raise. Nobody explained anything. My take-home went up far less than I expected.
A payroll nobody understands is a payroll nobody trusts. The auditors will interview workers about their pay.
Your mission: learn this vault from gross to net, fix what is wrong, and be able to explain any payslip to anyone. Ready?

cards.title: The journey of a rupee from gross to net

scenes.heading: Basic salary first
scenes.narration: Pay starts with basic salary. It matters more than its size suggests, because provident fund, gratuity and often overtime are calculated from it.

scenes.heading: Allowances build gross
scenes.narration: House rent, utilities, conveyance and other allowances are added to basic. Basic plus allowances, plus any overtime or arrears, gives gross pay for the month.

scenes.heading: Deductions take it to net
scenes.narration: From gross, payroll subtracts income tax withheld, the employee's provident fund share, the employee's EOBI share, loan instalments and any lawful recoveries. What remains is net pay, the amount in the bank.

scenes.heading: The employer pays more
scenes.narration: On top of gross, the employer pays its own provident fund share, its larger EOBI share, provincial social security for covered workers and a gratuity provision. Together that is the cost to company.

scenes.heading: Money owed to others
scenes.narration: Tax withheld and statutory contributions are not the company's money. They must be deposited on time, with returns filed, or the employer faces penalties.

cards.title: The monthly payroll cycle
cards.caption: Wages must be paid within the deadline in wage-payment law (traditionally a few days after the wage period ends, depending on establishment size; check your provincial law).

cards.question: At Noorpur, which of these is normally calculated as a percentage of basic salary rather than gross pay?
options: Net pay
Income tax withheld
The unpaid-leave deduction under a gross-based policy
The provident fund contribution
cards.explanation: Provident fund rules usually set contributions as a percentage of basic salary. That is why Bilal's finding of PF taken on gross for forty staff is an error. Income tax is worked out on taxable salary, not just basic.

cards.title: Building gross and getting to net
cards.body:
A common Pakistani structure (company practice, not law) sets house rent allowance at **45% of basic** and utilities at **10% of basic**.

| | PKR |
|---|---|
| Basic | 100,000 |
| House rent (45%) | 45,000 |
| Utilities (10%) | 10,000 |
| **Gross** | **155,000** |
| Provident fund, employee 10% of basic | −10,000 |
| EOBI, employee share | −400 |
| Income tax withheld | −9,000 |
| Loan instalment | −5,000 |
| **Net** | **130,600** |

The EOBI line assumes contributions on an illustrative minimum wage of PKR 40,000 at 1% for the employee; the tax figure is illustrative too. Use the currently notified wage and the current Finance Act slabs in real payroll.

cards.title: One payslip, four numbers
cards.caption: Cost to company here = gross + employer PF (10,000) + employer EOBI (5% of the PKR 40,000 illustrative wage = 2,000). Gratuity provision and social security, where applicable, add more.

items.label: Gross pay
items.detail: Basic plus house rent and utilities allowances

items.label: Net pay
items.detail: What reaches the employee's bank account

items.label: Cost to company
items.detail: Gross plus employer PF and employer EOBI

cards.title: Provident fund, gratuity, EOBI and social security
cards.body:
- **Provident fund (PF):** employee and employer each contribute a set % of basic (often 8.33% or 10%) to a trust run by trustees, separate from the company. A fund **recognised** by the tax authority gets tax advantages on contributions and profit, within limits. On exit the member receives the balance plus profit, under the fund's vesting rules.
- **Gratuity:** a lump sum for service. The Standing Orders rule is **30 days' wages for each completed year**, and a final part-year counts as a year only if it is **more than six months**. Many firms use last-drawn basic; the policy must state the base. An approved employer-contributory PF can replace gratuity under conditions in the law.
- **EOBI:** old-age pension scheme. Employer and employee contribute on a wage linked to the notified minimum wage, commonly **5% employer, 1% employee**.
- **Provincial social security:** the employer pays a % of wages for covered workers (generally those below a wage ceiling) for medical, sickness, maternity and injury benefits.

Rates and ceilings change: check the current law.

cards.front: Is provident fund money the company's money?
cards.back: No. It belongs to the members and sits in a trust managed by trustees, separate from the company's own accounts.

cards.front: 7 years 8 months' service, last basic PKR 80,000. Gratuity at 30 days per year?
cards.back: The 8 months exceed six, so count 8 years: 8 × 80,000 = PKR 640,000.
Four months does not exceed six, so 7 years: 7 × 80,000 = PKR 560,000.

cards.front: Who pays the larger EOBI share?
cards.back: The employer, commonly 5% against the employee's 1%, on a wage linked to the notified minimum wage.

cards.front: Does the employee contribute to provincial social security?
cards.back: Generally no. The employer contributes for covered workers, who then get medical and cash benefits from the provincial institution.
Funded: money set aside in an approved fund, often valued by an actuary. Unfunded: a provision in the company's books, paid from its own cash on exit.

cards.title: Double means double
cards.setting: Plant HR office, Sheikhupura. Ghulam sits across from you with a folder of payslips. Saima has the attendance register open.

lines.text: Plant workers on overtime are entitled to twice their ordinary rate under factories law. Ours were paid one times for six months.
Fifty workers, about twenty overtime hours each a month, ordinary rate about 180 rupees an hour. They were paid 180 instead of 360 for every overtime hour.
Can we fix it from next month and call it even? Arrears for six months will blow my plant budget.
If you only fix it from next month, the boys will take that as an insult. They worked those hours.
Run the numbers. Then decide what a fair, lawful fix looks like before Ghulam's WhatsApp group decides for us.

cards.title: Fixing the overtime underpayment
cards.situation: The shortfall is 180 rupees for each overtime hour: 50 workers × 20 hours × 6 months × PKR 180 = PKR 1,080,000. Tariq wants to correct the rate from next month only. Ghulam is waiting for an answer.

choices.text: Correct the rate from next month and quietly pay arrears only to workers who complain
choices.outcome: Word spreads within a day. Paying only those who complain is unfair, keeps the underpayment for everyone else, and turns into a grievance and an audit finding.

choices.text: Correct the rate and pay arrears in six instalments, explained to Ghulam and the workers in advance
choices.outcome: It respects the debt and protects the budget, and Ghulam may accept it. But wages already earned are owed now, and spreading them out without agreement risks a breach of wage-payment law.

choices.text: Correct the rate in the system, pay the full PKR 1,080,000 in arrears with a clear explanation on payslips, and add a rate check to the monthly variance review
choices.outcome: Ghulam takes the news to the floor and the go-slow talk stops. The law is met, workers see the error owned and repaid, and the control makes a repeat unlikely.

choices.text: Correct the rate from next month only, since the error was a system fault and not deliberate
choices.outcome: Intent does not reduce the debt. Workers were underpaid for hours they worked, and a labour inspector or auditor will treat it as unpaid wages.

cards.title: Tariq's January tax jump, explained
cards.body:
Employers must withhold tax from salary every month under the salary withholding section of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001. The method:

1. **Project** the employee's taxable salary for the whole tax year (July to June).
2. **Apply** the slabs in force for that year. They change through each Finance Act and normally apply from the first payroll of July, so check the current one.
3. **Spread** the annual tax over the months: annual tax ÷ 12.
4. **When pay changes**, recalculate: (new projected annual tax − tax already deducted) ÷ remaining months.

Tariq's projected annual tax was PKR 120,000, so 10,000 a month from July to December: 60,000 deducted. His January raise lifts projected annual tax to 150,000 (illustrative figures). For the 6 remaining months: (150,000 − 60,000) ÷ 6 = **PKR 15,000 a month**.

The whole year's extra tax falls into six months, so his take-home rises less than his raise. Explain this in the increment letter and nobody is surprised.

cards.question: From July to September an employee had PKR 6,000 a month withheld. A raise effective October lifts her projected annual tax to PKR 117,000. What should be withheld each month from October to June?
cards.explanation: Tax already deducted is 3 × 6,000 = 18,000. Remaining months October to June = 9. (117,000 − 18,000) ÷ 9 = 11,000. Dividing 117,000 by 12 ignores what was already deducted, and dividing it by 9 ignores the 18,000 already paid.

cards.title: Who handles what?
cards.prompt: Match each scheme or rule to what it does.

pairs.right: Holds employee and employer contributions plus profit, managed by trustees
Lump sum for service, traditionally 30 days' wages per completed year
Old-age pension and survivors' benefits funded mainly by employer contributions
Medical, sickness, maternity and injury benefits for covered workers
Employer deducts tax monthly on projected annual salary and deposits it
A share of company profits set aside for eligible workers under its own law

items.label: Calculation
items.right: Days of wages × years of service

cards.title: Final settlement, step by step
cards.prompt: Arrange the steps for settling a leaver's dues in a sensible order.
steps: Exit date recorded in HRIS before payroll cut-off
Clearance from departments: assets returned, loans confirmed
Calculate dues: salary to last day, leave encashment per policy, gratuity
Subtract lawful recoveries such as an outstanding staff loan, and tax
A second person checks and approves the settlement
Pay it with a written breakdown and a service certificate

cards.question: Which of these is part of Noorpur's cost of employing someone but never appears as a deduction on that employee's payslip?
options: The employee's provident fund share
Income tax withheld on salary
The employer's EOBI contribution
A staff loan instalment
cards.explanation: The employer's EOBI share (commonly 5%) is paid on top of gross, so it adds to cost to company without reducing net pay. The employee's PF share, tax and loan instalments are all deducted from gross.

cards.title: Controls that keep the vault locked
cards.body:
- **Variance review:** compare every department's total and headcount with last month. Any unexplained jump stops approval.
- **Segregation of duties:** the person who changes bank details or pay rates never releases the bank file.
- **Control totals:** the bank file total must equal the approved payroll net total.
- **Rate checks:** test overtime factors, PF % and allowance % after every system change.
- **Hourly rate:** convert the monthly ordinary wage with the divisor your policy states, such as 26 days × 8 hours.
- **Unpaid leave:** apply the divisor your policy states (for example gross ÷ 30 per day) consistently.
- **Confidential payslips:** each employee sees only their own.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Payroll Vault
items: Gross = basic + allowances + overtime and arrears; net = gross − tax, employee PF, employee EOBI, loans and other lawful deductions.
Cost to company adds the employer's PF, EOBI, social security and gratuity provision on top of gross.
Overtime for factory workers is at twice the ordinary rate; underpayments are unpaid wages and must be repaid.
Gratuity: 30 days' wages per completed year, with a final part-year counted only if it exceeds six months.
Salary tax: project the year, apply current slabs, and on any change spread (annual tax − tax deducted) over the remaining months.
Variance review, maker-checker, segregation of duties and control totals keep payroll trustworthy.

cards.prompt: Pick your own last payslip. Can you trace every line from basic to net, and name which contributions your employer pays on top that never appear as deductions? Which line would you struggle to explain to a worker on the shop floor?

quiz.question: What does gross pay mean on a monthly payslip?
options: Basic salary before allowances are added
The amount actually paid into the employee's bank account
Total earnings for the month before any deductions
Total earnings plus the employer's contributions
quiz.explanation: Gross is all earnings (basic, allowances, overtime, arrears) before deductions. The bank amount is net pay, and earnings plus employer contributions is closer to cost to company.

quiz.question: An officer's basic salary is PKR 60,000. Company policy sets house rent at 45% of basic and utilities at 10% of basic. What is her gross monthly pay?
quiz.explanation: House rent = 27,000 and utilities = 6,000, so gross = 60,000 + 27,000 + 6,000 = 93,000. PKR 87,000 leaves out utilities; PKR 66,000 leaves out house rent.

quiz.question: For the same officer (basic PKR 60,000, gross PKR 93,000), the PF rules set the employee contribution at 10% of basic. What should be deducted each month?
quiz.explanation: 10% of basic 60,000 = 6,000. PKR 9,300 is 10% of gross, the exact mistake Bilal found; PKR 12,000 adds the employer's share, which is not deducted from the employee.

quiz.question: How are EOBI contributions generally worked out?
options: On a wage linked to the notified minimum wage, with the employer paying the larger share
As a percentage of each employee's actual gross pay, shared equally by employer and employee
As a fixed amount paid only by employees who choose to join the scheme
As a percentage of company profits paid once a year into a workers' fund
quiz.explanation: EOBI contributions are calculated on a wage linked to the notified minimum wage, commonly 5% from the employer and 1% from the employee. A share of profits describes the separate workers' profit participation scheme.

quiz.question: A machine operator's ordinary wage works out to PKR 200 per hour. He worked 12 overtime hours this month. Applying the factories-law rule of twice the ordinary rate, what is his overtime pay?
quiz.explanation: Overtime rate = 2 × 200 = 400; 12 × 400 = 4,800. PKR 2,400 is single rate (Noorpur's error), PKR 3,600 is time-and-a-half and PKR 9,600 doubles the rate twice.

quiz.question: A worker leaves after 5 years and 7 months. Her last-drawn basic was PKR 50,000 and the policy pays gratuity of 30 days' basic per completed year, counting a final part-year of more than six months as a year. What is her gratuity?
quiz.explanation: Seven months is more than six, so count 6 years: 6 × 50,000 = 300,000. PKR 250,000 ignores the part-year; PKR 279,167 pro-rates it, which the rule does not do.

quiz.question: An employee had PKR 8,000 tax withheld each month from July to October (PKR 32,000 in total). From November a raise lifts his projected annual tax to PKR 132,000. What should be withheld each month from November to June?
quiz.explanation: (132,000 − 32,000) ÷ 8 remaining months = 12,500. PKR 11,000 is 132,000 ÷ 12, which ignores the lower deductions already made; PKR 16,500 divides the full annual tax by 8.

quiz.question: Noorpur's policy deducts unpaid leave at gross ÷ 30 per day. An officer on PKR 60,000 gross took 2 days of leave without pay. What is the deduction?
quiz.explanation: 60,000 ÷ 30 = 2,000 per day; 2 days = 4,000. PKR 3,871 uses a 31-day divisor and PKR 4,615 uses 26 days. Whichever divisor the policy states must be applied consistently.

quiz.question: Which statement about provincial social security is most accurate?
options: Employees and the employer contribute equally, and benefits are paid only on retirement
It is a voluntary scheme that only large employers choose to join
It replaces EOBI in every province, so employers pay only one of the two
The employer pays a % of wages for covered workers, who get medical and cash benefits
quiz.explanation: Provincial social security is generally funded by employer contributions for covered workers and provides medical, sickness, maternity and injury benefits. It sits alongside EOBI, which provides old-age benefits.

quiz.question: In the variance review, the warehouse department's payroll is 18% higher than last month with no change in headcount and no increments due. What should the payroll lead do?
options: Approve it, since headcount has not changed and the totals look broadly reasonable
Approve, and look into the difference after salaries are paid
Hold approval of that department until the increase is explained and evidenced
Reduce the department's total by 18% to match last month
quiz.explanation: An unexplained jump could be an overtime error, a wrong rate or fraud. Approving first means paying out money that may be wrong; cutting the total blindly could underpay people who earned the overtime.

sessions.title: Employment Law, Policies, Attendance and Leave
sessions.summary: Find your way through Pakistan's provincial labour-law landscape, from Standing Orders and minimum wage to working hours, leave and contract labour. Then turn the law into a handbook people actually follow, and manage attendance and leave fairly and consistently.
objectives: Describe how labour law is split between provinces and the federation after the 18th Amendment
Apply the core rules on minimum wage, working hours, overtime and leave, and know when to check provincial law
Place company policy correctly in the hierarchy of law, agreements, contracts and procedures
Write, launch and maintain policies and a handbook that employees understand and acknowledge
Manage attendance and leave consistently, including calculating the Bradford factor

cards.title: The 2014 handbook
cards.setting: Plant HR office, Sheikhupura. A dusty binder titled 'Employee Handbook 2014' sits open on Saima's desk. Ghulam has brought two loaders with him.

lines.text: Stage three. Payroll is cleaner, but the auditors will also test what Noorpur promises its people, and whether those promises meet the law.
These two are loaders from the labour contractor. Thirty-two thousand a month for full shifts, no EOBI card. Everyone knows that is below the provincial minimum wage.
And the handbook says sick leave is 'at the manager's discretion'. Supervisors refuse it whenever production is busy.
The loaders are the contractor's people, not ours. And I have a friend in Karachi who will send their handbook. Copy it, change the logo, done.
A Karachi handbook written for Sindh law, used in a Punjab plant? And contract workers below minimum wage inside our gate? Both would sink the audit.
Your mission at the Rulebook Archive: learn which rules apply to us, and rebuild a handbook that meets them. Where does our law even come from?

scenes.heading: The 18th Amendment
scenes.narration: In 2010 the 18th Amendment moved labour largely to the provinces. Since then Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan have each passed their own labour laws, at their own pace.

scenes.heading: Old laws still live
scenes.narration: Where a province has not replaced an older federal-era law, such as the Factories Act or the Standing Orders law of 1968, that older law generally continues to apply there, often with provincial amendments.

scenes.heading: The federal slice
scenes.narration: Federal labour laws still apply in the Islamabad Capital Territory. For union matters in establishments that operate across provinces, the federal Industrial Relations Act of 2012 and the National Industrial Relations Commission, the NIRC, come in.

scenes.heading: So, which law?
scenes.narration: Ask where the worker actually works, what kind of establishment it is, how many workers it has, and whether the person is a worker or a manager. The answers tell you which law applies.

scenes.heading: Your safe habit
scenes.narration: Never copy a policy from another province or company. Check the current law of your province, and get legal review before you publish anything.

cards.title: Landmarks in the rulebook
cards.caption: Many older laws have provincial successors or amendments. The year tells you when a law began, not what its current text says.

items.label: Factories Act
items.detail: Hours, overtime, leave, health and safety in factories

items.label: Payment of Wages Act
items.detail: When wages are paid and which deductions are allowed

items.label: Standing Orders law
items.detail: Terms of employment, classification, termination, misconduct

items.label: EOBI Act
items.detail: Old-age pensions and benefits for private-sector employees

items.label: Harassment law and 18th Amendment
items.detail: Workplace harassment protections; labour largely devolved to provinces

items.label: Federal Industrial Relations Act
items.detail: Unions and disputes in ICT and trans-provincial establishments

items.label: Harassment law amended
items.detail: Definitions and coverage of the 2010 law broadened

cards.question: After the 18th Amendment, where should Noorpur look first for the leave and working-hours rules that apply to its Sheikhupura plant?
options: Sindh's laws, because many large companies follow them
The federal laws for Islamabad Capital Territory
Punjab's labour laws, including older laws still in force there
The buyer's code of conduct, which replaces local law
cards.explanation: Labour is largely provincial, so the law of the province where the plant operates applies, including older laws that Punjab has not replaced. A buyer's code adds requirements but never replaces the law.

cards.title: The hierarchy of rules
cards.caption: A lower level may give more than a higher one, never less. A collective agreement (CBA settlement) binds the workers it covers until it is lawfully renegotiated.

items.label: Constitution and statutes
items.detail: Minimum wage, hours, leave, safety, discipline, harassment law

items.label: CBA settlements and awards
items.detail: Agreed terms for covered workers, often above the legal minimum

items.label: Employment contract
items.detail: Individual terms in the appointment letter

items.label: Company policy
items.detail: Rules the company sets for everyone, within the levels above

items.label: Procedures and guidelines
items.detail: How to apply the policy in practice

cards.title: The core rules you apply every week
cards.body:
These are the traditional baselines from factory and shop laws. Provinces have updated some of them, so **check your current provincial law** before relying on a number.

- **Minimum wage:** each province notifies its own (Islamabad by the federation), usually updated yearly. It applies to contract and daily-wage workers inside your premises too.
- **Hours:** adult factory workers traditionally up to **9 hours a day and 48 a week**, with rest intervals and a weekly holiday. Hours beyond these are overtime at **twice the ordinary rate**.
- **Annual leave:** **14 days** with full pay after 12 months' continuous service.
- **Casual leave:** **10 days** a year with full pay.
- **Sick leave:** **16 days** a year on **half pay**.
- **Public and festival holidays:** as notified.
- **Maternity:** differs by province and law, from 12 weeks under older law to longer periods under newer laws.
- **Who is covered:** Standing Orders protect **workers**; managers' terms come mainly from contract and policy.

Policy may give more, never less.

cards.title: Meets the law, or breaks it?
cards.prompt: Sort each practice found in the Noorpur review.

items.text: Annual leave of 20 days after a year's service for all staff
Overtime for plant workers paid at twice the ordinary rate
A regional manager's notice period set in his contract
Payroll updated to the new minimum wage from its notified effective date
Contract loaders inside the plant paid below the notified minimum wage
Sick leave refused whenever production is busy, as the handbook allows
A 300-worker plant not registered with EOBI
Plant workers routinely kept 56 hours a week with no overtime pay

cards.title: The contractor's people
cards.setting: Loading bay, 6 pm. Forty contract loaders finish the day shift. The contractor, Shakeel, waits by his motorbike.

lines.text: Forty loaders, PKR 32,000 each for a full month. If the notified minimum is 37,000, that is a 5,000 shortfall per person, every month.
Shakeel's contract says he is responsible for his workers. Not our problem.
They load our trucks, inside our gate, in our uniforms. The auditors will not care whose payroll they sit on.
Ghulam is right about the risk. A principal employer that lets a contractor underpay can be pulled into the liability, and the buyer treats it as our failure.
So, what do we do with Shakeel tomorrow morning?

cards.title: Fixing contract labour
cards.situation: Forty contract loaders have been paid PKR 32,000 a month for three months against an (assumed) notified minimum wage of PKR 37,000. None has EOBI or social security registration. The buyer's audit is in sixty days.

choices.text: Tell Shakeel to pay the minimum wage from next month and leave the past alone
choices.outcome: The future is fixed, but PKR 600,000 of underpayment (40 × 5,000 × 3) stays unpaid and unregistered. Auditors who interview the loaders will find it.

choices.text: Require Shakeel to pay arrears and the full minimum wage, register the workers, and prove it monthly with bank-paid salary records; write these duties into his contract
choices.outcome: The workers are paid what the law requires, the proof sits in your file, and the contract now lets you act if Shakeel slips. This is how a principal employer manages contract labour.

choices.text: Accept Shakeel's word that the workers are paid correctly and file his letter
choices.outcome: A letter is not evidence. Ghulam already knows the real figure, and so will the auditors when they speak to the loaders.

choices.text: Terminate Shakeel's contract at once and let the loaders go with him
choices.outcome: Forty people lose their jobs and their arrears with no fix. The underpayment that happened inside your gate is still your reputational problem, and the trucks stop.

cards.title: Policies that people actually follow
cards.body:
- **Policy:** what the company commits to and requires. *"Employees receive 20 days of annual leave."*
- **Procedure:** how it is done, step by step. *"Apply in the HRIS at least three days ahead; the supervisor approves within two days."*
- **Guideline:** advice that allows judgement. *"Managers are encouraged to spread leave across the year."*

A good handbook:
- Meets or beats the law of the province where people work.
- Matches the CBA settlement for covered workers.
- Is written plainly, with an **Urdu version** for the shop floor.
- Is **acknowledged** by each employee (signature or HRIS click) and explained in training.
- Has an owner, a version number and an **annual review date**.

A policy nobody has seen cannot be fairly enforced.

cards.title: Launching the new handbook
cards.prompt: Arrange the policy lifecycle steps for Noorpur's new handbook.
steps: Identify gaps against current provincial law and the CBA
Draft the policies in plain language
Legal review and consultation, including the union where required
Approve through the authority set by the board
Translate, communicate and train supervisors
Collect each employee's acknowledgment
Monitor use and review at least yearly

cards.back: Leave earned over time, for example a share of the annual entitlement each month, so balances grow as service grows.
Unused leave moved to the next year, within limits the law or policy sets.
Paying unused leave in cash, often at exit, at the rate and limit the policy states.
Absence approved but unpaid, deducted using the policy's divisor, such as gross ÷ 30 per day.
Absence without approval or notice. Repeated or prolonged absence can become a disciplinary matter.
A short, supportive conversation after each absence that checks wellbeing, reasons and any pattern.

cards.title: The Bradford factor: why short spells hurt more
cards.caption: Bradford factor = S² × D, where S is the number of separate absence spells and D the total days absent in the period. It flags frequent short absences. Exclude approved planned leave, maternity leave and workplace injuries.

items.label: Worker A: 1 spell, 10 days
items.detail: 1² × 10. One long illness, low disruption score

items.label: Worker B: 5 spells, 10 days
items.detail: 5² × 10. Same days, far more disruption

items.label: Worker C: 10 spells, 10 days
items.detail: 10² × 10. A pattern worth a supportive conversation

cards.question: Over six months a worker had 4 separate absence spells totalling 5 days. What is his Bradford factor?
cards.explanation: S² × D = 4² × 5 = 16 × 5 = 80. 20 is S × D, which ignores the squaring that makes frequent spells weigh more; 100 is 5² × 4, with S and D swapped.

cards.title: Which law covers it?
cards.prompt: Match each issue to the area of law that mainly governs it.

pairs.right: The province's minimum wage notification
The Standing Orders law in force in the province

pairs.left: Overtime and weekly hours in the plant
pairs.right: Factories law of the province

pairs.left: Union and collective bargaining across provinces
pairs.right: The federal Industrial Relations Act 2012
The EOBI Act

pairs.left: Deductions that may be made from wages
pairs.right: Wage-payment law

cards.title: The handbook rewrite at Noorpur
cards.body:
Saima and you compare the 2014 handbook with current Punjab law and the CBA settlement.

- **Sick leave:** "at manager's discretion" is replaced with the legal entitlement (or better), plus a rule that a medical certificate is needed for absences over two days. Supervisors can no longer refuse it for production reasons.
- **Annual leave:** the CBA gives plant workers 16 days. The draft said 14 (the legal baseline), so it is corrected to 16 for covered workers; the CBA prevails.
- **Contract labour:** a new section requires contractors to pay at least the minimum wage, register workers and provide monthly proof.
- **Language:** a plain Urdu version for the plant; supervisors trained in two short sessions.
- **Acknowledgment:** each worker signs; office staff click in the HRIS.

Tariq's Karachi handbook is politely returned. It cited Sindh laws that do not govern a Punjab plant.

cards.title: Fair attendance management
cards.body:
- **Link biometric data to rosters** in the HRIS so lateness and absence are measured against the actual shift.
- **Hold a return-to-work talk after every absence.** Most patterns improve once someone notices.
- **Use triggers, not instincts:** for example, a Bradford score or a number of spells that leads to a formal review.
- **Be consistent:** the same trigger for the favourite operator and the difficult one.
- **Never penalise protected absence:** approved statutory leave, maternity leave, or injury at work.
- **Look for causes:** Monday absences on one line may point to a supervisor, transport or a second job.

cards.question: A packer who joined eight months ago asks for a week of annual leave. Under the traditional baseline taught here, what is the position?
options: He is entitled to the full 14 days now, because entitlement starts on day one
He has not yet completed the 12 months' continuous service that earns annual leave, but casual leave is available
He gets no paid leave of any kind until he completes a year
He can take 14 days only if his supervisor agrees to waive the rule
cards.explanation: The traditional baseline grants 14 days of annual leave after 12 months' continuous service, while casual leave (10 days) is available during the year. Company policy may be more generous, for example by allowing leave to accrue monthly.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Rulebook Archive
items: Since the 18th Amendment, labour law is mostly provincial. Check the law where the worker works; federal law covers ICT and trans-provincial union matters.
Traditional baselines: 9 hours a day and 48 a week, overtime at double rate, 14 days annual, 10 casual and 16 sick (half pay). Verify the current provincial text.
Provinces notify minimum wages, and they apply to contract workers inside your gate. A principal employer must verify contractor compliance.
Law and CBA settlements sit above contracts and policies. Policies can give more, never less.
Policies need plain language, Urdu versions, acknowledgment, training, an owner and annual review.
Manage attendance with consistent triggers such as the Bradford factor (S² × D) and supportive return-to-work talks.

cards.prompt: Open your organisation's handbook. Find one rule that is vague (like 'at the manager's discretion'), one that may not match your province's current law, and one that employees have probably never read. What would you change first?

quiz.question: What did the 18th Amendment of 2010 change for labour law in Pakistan?
options: All labour laws were merged into one national labour code
Labour courts were abolished and replaced by company tribunals
Labour became largely a provincial subject
Private employers were exempted from labour laws for a decade
quiz.explanation: The amendment devolved labour largely to the provinces, which have since passed their own laws. There is no single national labour code, and labour courts and legal duties continue.

quiz.question: A labour contractor supplies daily-wage workers to a Lahore factory. Whose minimum wage rules apply to them, and do they apply at all?
options: No minimum wage applies, because they are not the factory's employees
The federal minimum wage for Islamabad applies to all contract workers
The contractor may set any wage the workers agree to in writing
Punjab's notified minimum wage, even though the contractor pays them
quiz.explanation: Minimum wage is notified by each province and covers workers employed through contractors. A worker's written agreement cannot waive the statutory minimum, and the Islamabad figure applies only in ICT.

quiz.question: A company policy grants fewer days of a type of leave than the applicable law requires. What is the legal position?
options: The legal entitlement applies; policy cannot give less than the law
The policy applies, because every employee acknowledged it in writing
The policy applies until the next annual review
Each manager decides which applies to his team
quiz.explanation: Statutes sit at the top of the hierarchy. A policy can improve on the law but cannot reduce statutory rights, even with an employee's signature.

quiz.question: During a walk-through you learn that a security contractor pays its guards at your site below the notified minimum wage. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Take no action, because the guards are employed by the contractor
Make the contractor pay the minimum and arrears, with monthly proof under the contract
Ask the guards to sign letters confirming they are fully satisfied with their pay and conditions
Replace the guards with a cheaper contractor before anyone notices
quiz.explanation: A principal employer should make contractors comply and verify it, because underpayment at its site creates legal and reputational risk. Satisfaction letters do not cure an unlawful wage, and switching contractors fixes nothing.

quiz.question: Which of these statements is a procedure rather than a policy?
options: Apply for annual leave in the HRIS at least three working days ahead
Employees are entitled to 20 days of annual leave a year
The company does not tolerate harassment of any kind
Overtime is paid at twice the ordinary rate for all plant workers on every shift
quiz.explanation: A procedure says how something is done, such as the steps and timing for applying. The other three state commitments or entitlements, which makes them policy.

quiz.question: In the last six months a worker had 3 separate absence spells totalling 6 days. What is her Bradford factor?
quiz.explanation: S² × D = 3² × 6 = 9 × 6 = 54. 18 is S × D without squaring; 108 squares the days instead of the spells (6² × 3); 36 squares the days and ignores the spells.

quiz.question: Under the traditional factory and shop law baselines taught in this stage, which paid annual leave entitlement applies after 12 months' continuous service?
options: 10 days
14 days
16 days
30 days
quiz.explanation: The traditional baseline is 14 days of annual leave with full pay after a year's continuous service. Ten days is the casual leave baseline and 16 days the sick leave baseline (on half pay). Always check current provincial law.

quiz.question: A regional sales manager leaving the company claims the Standing Orders law sets his notice period. Where should HR mainly look to settle his notice terms?
options: The Standing Orders law, which covers all employees equally, whatever their role
The CBA settlement for plant workers
The buyer's code of conduct
His employment contract and the company policy for managers
quiz.explanation: Standing Orders mainly protect workers, while managerial staff's terms come chiefly from their contracts and policy. A CBA settlement covers the workers it was negotiated for.

quiz.question: A packer has been absent on three of the last five Mondays, each time with a phone message. What should the supervisor do first?
options: Issue a final written warning for habitual absence
Hold a return-to-work talk to understand why and note the pattern
Deduct an extra day's pay for each Monday missed, as a deterrent to others
Ignore it, since each absence was reported by phone
quiz.explanation: A supportive return-to-work talk finds causes and signals that patterns are noticed, before any formal step under a consistent trigger. Jumping to a final warning or extra deductions is unfair and may be unlawful.

quiz.question: What most strengthens a company's ability to apply a new attendance policy fairly on the shop floor?
options: An Urdu version, supervisor training and signed acknowledgments
Publishing it on the intranet in English only
Approval by the board without consulting anyone
A strong opening statement from the CEO
quiz.explanation: People must be able to read, understand and confirm a policy before it can be fairly enforced. An English-only intranet page or board approval alone does not reach plant workers.

sessions.title: Employee Relations, Grievances and Fair Discipline
sessions.summary: Keep the peace on the shop floor by handling grievances quickly and fairly, running disciplinary cases that respect natural justice from show-cause notice to inquiry and decision, choosing proportionate penalties, and supporting the separate process the workplace-harassment law requires.
objectives: Tell grievances, disciplinary matters and harassment complaints apart and route each correctly
Apply the principles of natural justice to every disciplinary case
Draft a specific show-cause notice and run an impartial inquiry with a proper record
Choose proportionate, consistent penalties and tell termination apart from dismissal for misconduct
Explain the key duties the workplace-harassment law places on employers

cards.title: Thirty missing cartons
cards.setting: Plant floor, Sheikhupura. 11 pm, night shift. The loading-bay CCTV screen is frozen on a grey van.

lines.text: Stage four. Forty-five days to the audit. Tonight the Hearing Room opens without warning.
Thirty cartons of milk powder gone. The camera shows Faisal from dispatch loading a private van. I told him on the floor: you're fired, get out.
Faisal says he was loading a sample consignment on his supervisor's instruction. Fired in front of everyone without a hearing? The night shift is ready to stop the line.
And there's something else. A packing-line operator just sent me a WhatsApp voice note. She says her shift supervisor keeps sending her messages at night that make her afraid to come in.
Two serious matters, two different processes, one angry shop floor. Get either wrong and we lose the people, the case, and probably the audit.
Your mission tonight: make sure both are handled fairly. What does fair actually require?

scenes.heading: Know the case
scenes.narration: A person accused of misconduct must be told exactly what they are accused of: what, when, where, which rule, and what evidence exists. A vague charge cannot be answered.

scenes.heading: Be heard
scenes.narration: They must get a fair chance to reply, to see the evidence against them, to question witnesses and to bring their own, usually with a co-worker or union representative beside them.

scenes.heading: An unbiased judge
scenes.narration: Nobody should judge a case they are part of. The witness, the complainant or the manager who already announced the verdict cannot run the inquiry.

scenes.heading: Decide on evidence
scenes.narration: Findings must rest on evidence recorded in the inquiry, not on rumours, past grudges or pressure from the top.

scenes.heading: Proportion and reasons
scenes.narration: The penalty must fit the proven misconduct and the person's record, be consistent with similar cases, be given in writing with reasons, and allow an appeal.

cards.title: A fair disciplinary process
cards.caption: Minor penalties may follow a show-cause notice and reply. Major penalties, such as dismissal, need a full inquiry first.

items.label: Incident and fact-finding
items.detail: Secure evidence: CCTV, gate passes, stock records, first statements

items.label: Suspension if needed
items.detail: Pending inquiry, to protect evidence or safety. Not a punishment

items.label: Show-cause notice
items.detail: Specific allegations, rule breached, evidence, time to reply in writing

items.label: Reply considered
items.detail: If accepted, close or caution; if not, proceed to inquiry

items.label: Impartial inquiry
items.detail: Hearing, witnesses, cross-questioning, representative present, signed minutes

items.label: Findings and decision
items.detail: Inquiry officer finds facts; a separate authority decides the penalty

items.label: Written order and appeal
items.detail: Reasons stated; route and deadline for appeal given

cards.question: Tariq announced on the shop floor that Faisal is fired. Why does that make Tariq unsuitable to conduct Faisal's inquiry?
options: Plant managers are never allowed to take part in disciplinary matters
He has not yet received inquiry-officer training from HR
The union must always choose the inquiry officer
He has already declared a verdict, so he cannot be an unbiased judge
cards.explanation: Natural justice requires an unbiased decision-maker. Having announced the outcome, Tariq has prejudged the case. Managers can take part in discipline generally, and the union does not choose the inquiry officer.

cards.title: Grievance, discipline or harassment?
cards.prompt: Route each matter to the process it belongs in.

items.text: A worker says his night-shift allowance has not been paid for two months
An operator complains the canteen roster always gives her team the last slot
A storekeeper is seen on CCTV removing stock without a gate pass
A forklift driver is found asleep on duty for the third time
A machine operator refuses a lawful instruction from his supervisor and shouts abuse
A supervisor repeatedly sends a junior colleague unwelcome late-night messages
A manager suggests a promotion depends on an employee meeting him privately after hours

cards.title: Writing a show-cause notice that holds up
cards.body:
A show-cause notice (or charge sheet) is the foundation of the whole case. If it is vague, everything built on it can collapse.

**Include:**
- **Specific allegations:** what happened, date, time, place. *"On 14 October at about 10:40 pm you loaded 30 cartons of milk powder into vehicle LEB-xxxx without a gate pass."*
- **The rule or misconduct** it may amount to, such as theft or dishonesty under the Standing Orders list, or a named policy.
- **The evidence** relied on, and how the employee can see it.
- **Time to reply in writing**, as policy states (often several working days).
- **What happens next** if there is no reply or it is not satisfactory.
- **Suspension status**, if suspended, and the pay rules that apply.

**Avoid:** "your conduct has been unsatisfactory", conclusions ("you stole") before the inquiry, and bundling unrelated old complaints.

cards.title: Termination versus dismissal for misconduct
cards.caption: Mixing these up is one of the most common reasons an employer loses at the labour court.

items.label: Reason
items.left: Redundancy, closure, end of contract, other non-fault grounds
items.right: Proven misconduct such as theft or insubordination

items.label: Process
items.left: Notice or pay in lieu as law and contract require

items.label: Written order
items.right: States the proven charges and reasons for penalty

items.label: Exit dues
items.left: Notice, gratuity and other benefits per law and policy
items.right: Dues per law and policy; take advice before withholding anything

cards.title: The night shift waits
cards.setting: Plant HR office, 11:40 pm. Through the window you can see the night shift gathered by the canteen, machines idle.

lines.text: Give me something to tell them. Either Faisal gets a fair hearing or nobody touches a machine till morning.
I'm not taking back my words in front of the whole shift. A thief is a thief.
The CCTV shows loading. It doesn't show who authorised it. Faisal's supervisor hasn't been asked anything yet.
Tariq, nobody is calling him innocent or guilty yet. That is exactly the point. What do we put in writing tonight?

cards.title: Undoing an on-the-spot firing
cards.situation: Faisal was told on the floor that he is fired. There is CCTV of loading but no record of who authorised it. The night shift has stopped work, and Ghulam wants an answer now.

choices.text: Issue a dismissal letter tonight attaching the CCTV clip, since the evidence is clear
choices.outcome: The CCTV shows loading, not theft or authority. A dismissal without charge, reply or inquiry is likely to be overturned, and the shift sees management deciding first and asking later.

choices.text: Let Faisal return to his normal duties while HR asks around informally over the next few weeks
choices.outcome: It calms the floor, and avoids prejudging him. But with no formal process the case drifts, the dispatch area and records stay open to him, and no one can act on what is found.

choices.text: Ask Ghulam to persuade Faisal to resign quietly so nobody loses face
choices.outcome: A pressured resignation can be challenged as a forced dismissal, and the real question of who took the cartons is never answered.

choices.text: Confirm in writing that no dismissal has been made, suspend Faisal pending inquiry, issue a specific show-cause notice, and name an independent inquiry officer; tell Ghulam the steps
choices.outcome: The line restarts within the hour. Faisal's rights are protected, the evidence is safe, and the case can now end in any outcome the facts support, including dismissal if theft is proved.

cards.title: Handling an individual grievance
cards.prompt: Put the stages of a fair grievance procedure in order.
steps: Worker raises the issue informally with the immediate supervisor (or the next level if the supervisor is involved)
If unresolved, the worker submits a written grievance to HR
HR acknowledges it in writing and investigates the facts
A meeting is held where the worker explains, with a representative if wanted
A written decision with reasons is given within the policy's time limit
The worker may appeal to a higher authority, and beyond that to the statutory forum

cards.title: Running the inquiry
cards.body:
- **Inquiry officer:** independent of the incident, senior enough, trained. Never the complainant, a witness or a manager who has prejudged.
- **Notice of hearing:** date, place, right to bring a co-worker or union representative.
- **Evidence in the open:** management witnesses speak in the employee's presence; the employee may cross-question them and call their own.
- **Documents:** the employee may see what is relied on, such as CCTV, gate registers and stock records.
- **Minutes:** recorded at each sitting and signed by those present. Urdu is fine; accuracy matters more.
- **Report:** a finding on each charge, with reasons drawn from the evidence. The inquiry officer recommends; the competent authority decides.
- **Parallel police case:** an internal inquiry can usually proceed, because it asks a different question to a lower standard of proof. Take legal advice.
- **Time:** move briskly. Long suspensions are unfair and costly.

cards.title: Spot the breach
cards.prompt: Match each flawed practice to the principle it breaks.

pairs.right: Know the case: allegations must be specific enough to answer

pairs.left: Witnesses interviewed privately and never produced
pairs.right: Right to be heard, including testing the evidence

pairs.left: The complainant's own manager runs the inquiry
pairs.right: An unbiased decision-maker

pairs.left: Dismissed for a first late arrival of ten minutes
pairs.right: Proportionality of penalty

pairs.left: Two workers, same proven offence, same record: one dismissed, one warned
pairs.right: Consistency

pairs.left: Dismissal letter gives no reasons and no appeal route
pairs.right: Reasoned decision and right of appeal

cards.title: Choosing a proportionate penalty
cards.caption: Consider the proven misconduct, the live record, mitigation and how similar cases were handled. Serious misconduct can justify a major penalty even on a clean record.

items.label: Minor, with live warnings
items.detail: Escalate in steps, such as a final written warning

items.label: Serious, with live warnings
items.detail: Dismissal is likely to be proportionate

items.label: Minor, clean record
items.detail: Counselling or a first written warning

items.label: Serious, clean record
items.detail: Major penalty possible; weigh service and mitigation

cards.back: The Protection against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act 2010, amended in 2022 to broaden its definitions and coverage. Check the current text.
Employers must adopt the code of conduct under the law and display it prominently, in English and Urdu, where people work.
Each organisation forms a committee of three members, at least one of whom is a woman, to hear complaints.
To the organisation's inquiry committee, or directly to the Ombudsperson (federal or provincial) set up under the law.
Proceedings are confidential, and the complainant and witnesses must be protected from any retaliation.
Receive the complaint respectfully, explain the options, pass it to the committee promptly and support interim measures such as changing reporting lines.

cards.question: Saima received the packing operator's complaint about her supervisor by WhatsApp voice note. What should HR do next?
options: Ask the supervisor for his side first, before deciding whether a complaint exists
Tell her to resolve it directly with the supervisor, then return if it continues
Hold it until the audit is over, to avoid an incident appearing in the records
Explain her options, refer the complaint promptly to the inquiry committee in confidence, and guard against retaliation
cards.explanation: A harassment complaint goes to the committee, which runs its own process, while the complainant learns she can also go to the Ombudsperson. Approaching the accused first, pushing her to confront him or delaying all risk harm and breach the law.

cards.title: How Faisal's case ended
cards.body:
The show-cause notice set out the 14 October loading, the missing gate pass and the CCTV. Faisal replied that his supervisor, Naveed, had told him by phone to load "samples for a distributor".

An inquiry officer from the Lahore finance team, with no link to the plant, held three sittings. Ghulam attended with Faisal. Naveed was questioned in Faisal's presence and denied any instruction, but call records showed a two-minute call from Naveed at 10:31 pm, and the van belonged to Naveed's cousin.

**Findings:** the charge against Faisal was not proved; he had acted on an instruction. A new charge was framed against Naveed, with its own notice, reply and inquiry. Naveed was dismissed for theft and dishonesty in a reasoned written order, with an appeal route.

Tariq's on-the-spot firing would have punished the wrong man and freed the real one.

cards.title: Writing a decision letter that survives challenge
cards.body:
- **Refer to the notice, reply and inquiry report** by date.
- **State each charge and whether it was proved**, with the key evidence.
- **Explain the penalty:** why it fits, what mitigation was weighed, and how it compares with past cases.
- **Give the effective date**, the dues payable and how they will be paid.
- **State the appeal route and deadline.**
- **Warnings carry a 'live' period** set by policy, often 12 months. An expired warning should not be used to escalate a new case.
- Keep the tone factual. No insults, no moral lectures.

cards.question: A storekeeper's written reply to a show-cause notice denies taking stock. His manager wants to dismiss him on the strength of the notice and reply alone. What is the right course?
options: Hold a full inquiry first, because a major penalty such as dismissal needs one
Dismiss him, because he had the chance to reply in writing
Give him a minor penalty instead, since a dismissal is now ruled out
Close the case, because a written denial ends the matter
cards.explanation: Minor penalties may follow a notice and reply, but a major penalty needs a full inquiry where evidence is tested. A denial does not close the case, and it does not rule out dismissal if the inquiry proves the charge.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Hearing Room
items: Route each matter correctly: grievances to the grievance procedure, misconduct to discipline, harassment complaints to the inquiry committee or Ombudsperson.
Natural justice: specific charges, a real chance to reply and test evidence, an unbiased judge, decisions on evidence, proportionate and consistent penalties, reasons and appeal.
Major penalties need a full inquiry by an independent officer; the inquiry officer finds facts and a separate authority decides.
Termination for non-fault reasons and dismissal for misconduct follow different rules. Never confuse them.
The harassment law requires a displayed code of conduct, a three-member committee with at least one woman, confidentiality and protection from retaliation.

cards.prompt: Recall a disciplinary case you have seen or heard about. Which principle of natural justice was weakest: the charge, the hearing, the independence of the judge, the evidence, or the proportionality of the penalty? What would you do differently?
